evaluation.positioning_hook: A McGill student pulled into a Montreal mob favor is ordered to befriend a boss’s son, then gets trapped between family loyalty, blackmail, and a murder he can’t outrun.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is easy to grasp and the mob-school collision gives it a clean commercial engine. The audience is narrower than a broad four-quadrant crime show because the tone is specific and the Montreal/McGill setting is more premium-drama than mass-procedural.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early: Jimmy is forced into proximity with Nicky and Charlie, and the pilot keeps restating the pressure through the restaurant, the flowers, and the dead body. The opening teaser and the final reveal make the series engine legible in one pass.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jimmy has a strong contradiction: ambitious student, loyal son, and increasingly compromised operator. Dom, Nicky, Zoey, and Charlie all have playable edges, though Jimmy is still doing most of the heavy lifting as the series anchor.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Montreal setting, bilingual texture, and university/mob overlap give the script a fresher lane than a generic North American crime pilot. The voice is confident, but the underlying mob pressure-cooker is still familiar enough that the originality comes more from setting and social detail than from form.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The pilot is built on escalating pressure: the flowers, the recruitment, the surveillance, Mark’s discovery, and the murder cover-up all keep tightening the vise. The final squash-court button gives the episode a clean aftershock and a reason to keep going.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea of a college kid being used as a bridge into a mob family is immediately understandable and ownable. It feels fresher because the script ties that engine to McGill, suburban Montreal, and a family-business ecosystem rather than a generic gangster world.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world feels lived-in: the restaurant hierarchy, the barbershop cash route, the bilingual campus, the publicist/media layer around Frank, and the domestic pressure at Maria’s house all generate story. The pilot suggests a social ecosystem with multiple pressure points, not just a single crime plot.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a sharp tonal mix of menace, domestic awkwardness, and deadpan comedy, especially in the restaurant scenes and the family dinners. The white roses, the squash-court banter, and the mob guys’ petty behavior give it a distinct flavor rather than a generic grim crime tone.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real seeds here beyond the pilot plot: Frank’s public image, Charlie’s proximity, Zoey’s ambitions, Maria’s fragility, and the internal politics of the crew. The script hints at a larger social and emotional map, though the pilot still foregrounds the immediate crime engine.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jimmy/Zoey, Jimmy/Mark, Jimmy/Nicky, Dom/Luca, Dom/Rocco, and Jimmy/Maria all produce distinct energy, and the restaurant functions like a relationship hub. The ensemble is strong enough that multiple pairings can generate story without collapsing back to the lead every time.

lead_characters.name: Jimmy Basso
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, white/Italian-Canadian, McGill student, working-class family ties.
lead_characters.hook: Jimmy is a smart, angry, overextended young man trying to keep his life in separate boxes: school, his mother, Zoey, and the mob pressure he keeps pretending is temporary. He reads as the kind of guy who wants a clean future but keeps making morally expensive choices in the present, and the pilot steadily turns his self-control into the central suspense engine.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Imperioli in The Sopranos or Jesse Plemons in Breaking Bad — a role that lets an actor play intelligence, panic, loyalty, and self-disgust in the same scene. The part offers a long runway of internal conflict, escalating criminal compromise, and emotional fracture.

lead_characters.name: Dom Faraldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Italian-Canadian, mob captain, family patriarch.
lead_characters.hook: Dom is a polished, paternal mob boss who can switch from warmth to threat without changing his volume. He’s dangerous because he understands image, family, and leverage, and the pilot gives him enough charm and cruelty to feel like a long-term power center.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave James Gandolfini in The Sopranos or Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad so much acting territory — authority, vulnerability, and menace all living in the same body. It’s a prestige-gangster part with real scene-stealing range.

lead_characters.name: Nicky Faraldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, Italian-Canadian, overweight, Dom’s son, college-age.
lead_characters.hook: Nicky is comic, insecure, and more observant than he first appears, which makes him dangerous in a different way than the older guys. He wants status and approval, but the pilot keeps hinting that he’s also the one most likely to misread the room and expose the family’s rot.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Michael Imperioli’s Christopher Moltisanti or Jonah Hill in a darker register — a role that lets an actor toggle between insecurity, bravado, and sudden menace. The part has room for big behavior and real pathos.

lead_characters.name: Zoey Magliani
lead_characters.hook: Zoey is a hustler with real momentum: she can sell a pitch, chase a client, and build a future while still feeling emotionally tethered to Jimmy’s instability. She’s not just the girlfriend; she’s the pilot’s clearest counterweight to Jimmy’s drift, and her ambition gives the show a modern, professional texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Aimee Lou Wood in Sex Education or Molly Gordon in The Bear a chance to be funny, vulnerable, and strategically sharp all at once. It’s a strong contemporary female part with both charm and engine.

lead_characters.name: Maria Basso
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, Jimmy’s mother, fragile, medically compromised.
lead_characters.hook: Maria is a wounded, emotionally dependent mother whose small victories and lies carry real weight in Jimmy’s life. Her fragility gives the pilot its domestic stakes, and the white-roses beat turns her into a pressure point the mob can exploit without ever entering the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of emotionally loaded mother role that gave Frances McDormand in Olive Kitteridge or Lorraine Bracco in The Sopranos real awards-level material. The part offers grief, denial, tenderness, and humiliation in close-up.

lead_characters.name: Frank Byron
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, wealthy, politically ambitious, public-facing lawyer.
lead_characters.hook: Frank is a polished public figure whose interview scenes show him managing image as carefully as any mobster manages territory. He’s not the pilot’s center, but he adds a parallel power structure and a public/private hypocrisy that broadens the show’s world.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Matthew Macfadyen in Succession or Michael Stuhlbarg in The Looming Tower a chance to play intelligence under pressure and image management as performance. It’s a prestige supporting part with political and domestic stakes.

lead_characters.name: Charlie Byron
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, Frank’s son, McGill student, privileged, socially polished.
lead_characters.hook: Charlie looks like the clean version of the world Jimmy wants: educated, composed, and socially protected. The pilot uses him as both a target and a mirror, and the final scene suggests he may be more curious about Jimmy than his family would like.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Paul Dano in Little Miss Sunshine or Will Poulter in The Bear a chance to play charm with a shadow underneath it. It’s a deceptively light part that can deepen into something more complicated.

lead_characters.name: Mark
lead_characters.hook: Mark is the friend who keeps trying to stay normal while the story gets more dangerous around him. He’s funny, needy, and ultimately vulnerable, which makes him a useful emotional barometer and a credible casualty of Jimmy’s double life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Adam Pally in Happy Endings or Alex Wolff in Hereditary a chance to be funny and then suddenly heartbreaking. It’s a strong supporting part with real turn potential.

lead_characters.name: Rocco
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s, large, physically imposing, mob enforcer.
lead_characters.hook: Rocco is the blunt instrument in the room, but the pilot gives him enough presence that he feels like more than muscle. He’s the guy who can turn a conversation into a threat just by standing up, which makes him a reliable source of tension in every scene.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Vincent Pastore in The Sopranos or Michael Madsen in Reservoir Dogs a chance to dominate scenes with physical authority and deadpan menace. It’s a pure character-actor part with intimidation value.

lead_characters.name: Luca Biello
lead_characters.hook: Luca is the quieter power in the room, the one who watches, calculates, and lets other people make noise. He gives the mob world a colder, more managerial edge and suggests a deeper hierarchy beneath Dom’s charisma.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Kelly in House of Cards or Giancarlo Esposito in Better Call Saul a chance to play controlled intelligence and quiet threat. It’s a precision supporting role for an actor who can do a lot with stillness.

lead_characters.name: Corrado
lead_characters.hook: Corrado is the nervous weak link, the guy whose fear is always visible before the consequences arrive. The pilot uses him as both comic pressure relief and a liability, which makes his eventual collapse feel inevitable and tragic in the same breath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Steve Buscemi in Boardwalk Empire or Paul Walter Hauser in Black Bird a chance to play panic, shame, and volatility. It’s a juicy supporting part for an actor who can make weakness feel dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Cleo
lead_characters.hook: Cleo is the image manager who understands that politics, family, and optics are all the same game. She’s one of the pilot’s clearest signs that the show is about public performance as much as criminal power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Sarah Snook in Succession or Jodie Comer in The White Princess a chance to play intelligence, pressure, and social control. It’s a sharp, modern supporting role with bite.

lead_characters.name: Murphy
lead_characters.hook: Murphy is the loose cannon in the crew, the one who says the thing everyone else is trying not to say. He adds volatility and dark comic energy, but the pilot also makes him feel like a real threat when the violence escalates.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire or Jack Huston in Fargo a chance to play combustible, unpredictable energy. It’s a scene-chewing supporting part with danger built in.

lead_characters.name: Nadia Belanger
lead_characters.hook: Nadia is the media conduit through which Frank’s public image gets built and tested. She’s not just a reporter; she’s a pressure system, and the interview scenes make her feel like someone who can expose the gap between image and reality.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Carrie Coon in The Leftovers or Sarah Goldberg in Barry a chance to be smart, skeptical, and scene-steadying. It’s a compact but high-functioning supporting role.

lead_characters.name: T
lead_characters.hook: T is the faceless endpoint of Murphy’s violence, introduced as a professional who treats murder like a transaction. He’s brief but memorable, and the anonymity makes him feel like a larger criminal ecosystem is waiting offscreen.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire or Stephen Root in No Country for Old Men a chance to make a small amount of screen time feel loaded. It’s a compact, memorable hitman part.

notable_requirements: Montreal streets and suburban house exterior
McGill campus squash courts, locker room, workout room, pay phones
restaurant back room, dining room, and bathroom

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic editorial inserts and possible background cleanup.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical gun handling, blood makeup, bruising, corpse handling, and a few impact beats.

rights_flags.detail: Frank Byron’s political-media storyline references Edwin Muskie by name in the interview scene.
Twitter is shown as part of Frank Byron’s image management.
McGill is prominently used as a real university setting.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Serialized crime drama with a campus-to-mob pressure engine and ongoing family/power fallout.

budget.note: Contemporary urban production with a modest location footprint, no VFX load, and only minor practical violence. The main cost drivers are night exteriors, restaurant coverage, and a few additional company moves.

casting.note: Jimmy has to carry intelligence, panic, romantic credibility, and criminal pressure, while Dom, Nicky, Zoey, and Charlie all need distinct chemistry. The bilingual Montreal texture also narrows the pool if the production wants that authenticity on camera.

development.note: The pilot’s engine is clear, but the Frank Byron political-media thread and the Jimmy/Zoey/Mark triangle create a broader ensemble shape that will need disciplined series focus. The buyer conversation will center on which relationship is the true long-term spine.

comp_set.title: Bad Blood
comp_set.why_it_comps: Canadian mob-world storytelling with family, business, and criminal hierarchy colliding in a contemporary urban setting.

comp_set.title: The Sopranos
comp_set.why_it_comps: The family-first criminal ecosystem, dark humor, and domestic pressure around organized crime feel directly adjacent in tone and character behavior.

comp_set.title: Snowfall
comp_set.why_it_comps: A young lead getting pulled deeper into a criminal system while trying to preserve a normal life gives it the same escalating moral trap.

comp_set.title: Banshee
comp_set.why_it_comps: The propulsive crime pressure, bruising violence, and heightened character energy fit the same serialized, adult-genre lane.

comp_set.title: Succession
comp_set.why_it_comps: The public-image politics around Frank Byron and the family power dynamics echo the same prestige-drama appetite for status, optics, and betrayal.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige crime dramas with family dysfunction, moral compromise, and a strong sense of place.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but with strong female appeal through Zoey/Maria and the relationship drama; urban, streamer-native, prestige-drama viewers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, a recurring restaurant/campus world, modest stunt and blood work, and an 8-episode serialized season assumption keep this in the mid-tier range.

types_of_buyers: streamer original drama teams building adult crime slates
premium cable buyers looking for a character-first mob series
indie producers with access to Canadian tax incentives and bilingual talent
buyer teams seeking a prestige male-lead vehicle with ensemble support
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of adult crime drama with family and image-management pressure, but the Montreal/McGill specificity gives it a cleaner identity than a generic mob show. The series has enough relationship energy to appeal to buyers who want both serialized crime and domestic character play.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone series rather than a franchise engine; no clear spinoff vector emerges beyond the main Jimmy/Dom world.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Montreal gives the crime world a fresh address.
strengths.what_it_means: The setting helps the show stand out in a crowded mob-drama market because it feels specific rather than imported. Buyers looking for a prestige crime series with a regional identity and bilingual texture will notice that immediately.
strengths.evidence: McGill, Montreal streets, French dialogue, and the Del Fiacco restaurant ecosystem all anchor the pilot in place.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jimmy is built as a pressure-cooker lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role can carry a long-running series because his intelligence, anger, and divided loyalties create repeatable conflict. That makes the project attractive to actors and buyers who want a lead with both emotional access and criminal escalation.
strengths.evidence: He’s juggling school, Zoey, his mother, and Dom’s demands while trying to keep his life from collapsing.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The pilot has a clean, escalating engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The flowers, the recruitment, the surveillance, and the murder cover-up create a strong episode-to-episode propulsion that is easy to pitch. That kind of clarity helps a buyer see the series order and the pilot order at the same time.
strengths.evidence: The white roses return as a threat, Mark is pulled into the room, and the final body disposal locks the season’s moral stakes in place.

strengths.what_it_means: Multiple relationship pairings can generate scenes, which is a real asset for a serialized drama. Buyers can see story value beyond the lead because Dom, Nicky, Zoey, Maria, and Charlie all create different kinds of pressure.
strengths.evidence: Jimmy/Zoey, Jimmy/Mark, Jimmy/Nicky, Dom/Luca, and Jimmy/Maria all play as distinct engines.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone balances menace with dark humor.
strengths.what_it_means: That tonal mix broadens the show’s appeal and gives it a more premium, character-driven feel than a straight crime procedural. It also gives directors and actors room to play subtext, which is attractive in the marketplace.
strengths.evidence: The restaurant banter, the vape monologue, the squash-court jokes, and the family dinner scenes all sit beside genuine threat.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable crime series with a strong lead role, a specific Montreal identity, and a production footprint that stays in the mid-tier lane. The pilot’s real commercial value is that it combines prestige-drama family pressure with a propulsive mob engine, which makes it legible to both streamer buyers and actor-driven packaging conversations.

items.area: The Frank Byron thread broadens the show fast.
items.detail: The pilot opens a parallel political-image storyline with Frank, Cleo, Nadia, and Charlie, which adds texture but also creates a second center of gravity. A buyer will notice that the series is flirting with both mob drama and public-facing political drama in the same hour.

items.area: Jimmy carries most of the series weight.
items.detail: The pilot gives Jimmy the clearest want, the biggest reversals, and the strongest emotional contradictions, while several supporting players are still defined mainly by their function around him. That is fine for a pilot, but it means the ensemble promise is still more visible than the ensemble depth.

items.area: The violence spikes hard in the back half.
items.detail: Mark’s death, Corrado’s killing, and the body disposal push the episode into a much darker register than the earlier domestic and comic material. That tonal escalation is effective, but it narrows the buyer pool to platforms comfortable with mature crime content and sustained brutality.

items.area: The bilingual texture is specific, not universal.
items.detail: The French dialogue and Montreal specificity are a strength, but they also make the show feel less plug-and-play for buyers looking for a broadly Americanized crime series. The authenticity is part of the appeal, and part of the audience-shaping constraint.

issues.headline: The main buyer conversation will be about focus: the pilot has enough world and side-thread energy to feel rich, but the Frank Byron material and the Jimmy-centered mob plot are both reaching for attention. The other friction point is tonal and content-based — once the episode turns to murder and cleanup, the show is firmly in mature premium-drama territory.
